title: Giorgia Meloni a Pulp Podcast. | Pulp Podcast #51
transcript:
Welcome back to Pulp Podcast, everyone
Today's a very special episode for us, not only because we have a highly distinguished
institutional guest, but also because this is
a major milestone for us. Over the past two years, we've tried to build a new
space for debate, including political debate, because we strongly believe there is
an audience that engages with politics without relying on traditional media So, having the Italian Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni, here today is a great
opportunity and, once again, a major milestone. So without further ado, please
welcome Giorgia Meloni. Welcome Thank you, thank you. Good afternoon. The Iran issue. What’s Italy's
official stance on the Middle East and on Trump? Well, Italy's official stance is
the one we’ve already presented in Parliament: Italy is not taking part in this attack
against Iran, and has no intention of doing so What we're trying to do, given the situation,
is to work towards de-escalation We're helping the Gulf countries defend
themselves, as they're strategic partners, and especially because, as you know,
tens of thousands of Italians are in the region, along with 2,000 troops stationed there.
Then of course, we're working to address the consequences of the conflict,
which are, for Italy, mainly related to security and the economy.
We need to manage and minimize them as much as possible.
But if you ask me what I think about the US - Israeli attack on Iran,
this is a very complex issue because I'm obviously concerned about
what is clearly a crisis of international law, which is now evident to everyone. It's the result
of a long process, let's put it this way. But there have been some
decisive moments that have led to a world where unilateral decisions are increasingly common.
Actions taking place outside international law. The point is that we are now living in a world
where you have to choose between scenarios that are, let's say, all quite
unsettling. In the specific case of Iran, the American position is that it hasn't
been possible to reach an agreement on Iran’s nuclear program. You know that there are
many independent experts who say that Iran has reached a uranium enrichment level
of around 60%. 60% is far beyond what is needed for civilian
purposes. It's close to what is required to make a nuclear weapon.
So of course, you have to assess the situation both in terms of what war would entail, and what the alternative might be. Let's be clear,
nobody likes war. But what's the possible alternative?
Clearly, none of us would feel safe with an Ayatollah-led regime armed with
a nuclear weapon. Especially considering they also have long-range missiles. It'd be
very dangerous.So, from a government standpoint the question is:
to put it simply What is more dangerous? A war today to prevent
Iran from getting a nuclear bomb, or the risk of that regime
attacking us tomorrow with one? Obviously the situation is complex.
The point is, since I wasn't at the negotiation table, I don’t have enough
information to either confirm or deny what the Americans say about the impossibility
of reaching an agreement with Iran. So we continue to pursue what I believe
is the only reasonable path, which is trying to reach an agreement where
Iran agrees to use uranium exclusively for civilian purposes. I don't know
if that's still a possibility at this moment but that is clearly the direction
we're pursuing. Italy's position is aligned with that of most European countries.
And it's the path we have to continue working on. But don't you think that there's a risk of a situation
similar to what happened with Russia and Ukraine? They said we had to wait
for mediation between Putin and Zelensky... And later we found out that Zelensky
didn't want an agreement. We know what happened. I mean, I wouldn't say that
 Zelensky didn't want an agreement... at this point it seems that Russia didn't want it. Yes, I agree with you but that's how Putin justified his actions.
And Trump might do the same. It's not about justifying, It's about verifying.
That said, in this specific case, in this situation,
even turning a blind eye and pretending nothing's happening--
In my opinion, the question isn't: "Do you like war or peace?"
Come on, guys. Politics is a bit more complex than that.
So, even if we decided to ignore the situation or openly condemn the attack
without actually knowing for sure whether there was a possibility or not...
What we know is that we've been trying to reach an agreement with Iran
for decades. We haven't been able to. So maybe there are elements
that suggest there is a real problem. Why would you enrich uranium up to 60%
if it’s for civilian purposes? We do have a problem
We can ignore it, but the problem's there. Yeah, that's why I'd be inclined
to take a stance on the US too. Because as you said,
international law is at risk right now. Against the US? You would take a stance
against the US? That's what I was talking about.
That is also a dangerous scenario. It's dangerous for you. Not for them.
So clearly, as the Prime Minister of Italy, I'm sure
you’ll understand that if I don’t have certainty, given that the safety of Italian
citizens is at stake--It's not that I'm a coward, or that I'm not clear-headed
or that I lack courage. I have to make more difficult assessments
than most people. Because if you make a mistake
nothing really happens If I make a mistake there are consequences.
And other people pay the price. About the lack of information, what
could other countries-- - I'm speaking too informally, I'm sorry.
- Please, don't worry about that. How can single countries find reliable
information amid all these events? Because of course someone can say
"I got this information", but-- Every time I discussed the topic
with the Americans, they said they were trying to reach an agreement.
I haven't had the chance to talk with Iran. From a strategic point of view,
it's really difficult to fully grasp the US position. Last summer Trump said
"We’ve gotten rid of the nuclear threat". So what now? Defense Minister Crosetto,
while speaking in Parliament, gave a very down to earth speech. He said
“Let’s be clear about who we are." "this is Italy. We are not a major global power.
We can play a role in de-escalation". How can we contribute to de-escalation? Clearly, through diplomacy. Guys, you have to consider
that we live in a time when the United Nations is not being effective.
And that is the core of the problem. Everybody talks about international law,
but who is supposed to enforce it? The United Nations.
So is it a problem or not, if a member of the UN Security Council invades a neighboring
country with the aim of annexation and nothing happens? Is it a problem if,
speaking of Iran, just a few months ago, after the Iranian regime had violently
suppressed peaceful killing thousands, an Iranian representative
was appointed vice chair of a UN commission on violence?
Is there a problem or not? This is the system of international law
we're talking about. One thing is on paper, one thing is reality.
If we talk about reality, the situation is much more complex.
What Italy can do--and I'm a bit more ambitious than Minister Crosetto
regarding Italy's role, is to use its credibility
and its presence in the Mediterranean. We're a key country in the Mediterranean region.
We have strong diplomatic capabilities. We have good relations with
 many of the key players in this scenario. Including all the Gulf countries.
You may recall that just a few months ago I attended the Gulf Cooperation Council
,as a guest of honor. I believe that two countries can play
a key diplomatic role in this scenario: Turkey and India. Because they have channels
of communication
and they are respected. Turkey is very much affected... And the Indian Prime Minister, was able to ensure the safe passage
of ships through the Strait of Hormuz. And of course, we maintain strong relations
with the US and with our European partners. One of Italy’s initiatives
has been to establish coordination with France Germany, and the UK, to try to align
the European position. Because the more unified your position is,
the greater your impact on the geopolitical stage. But the main role we can play here,
is a diplomatic one. I think the Israel issue has contributed
to these problems with international law.
Meaning that along with other situations, it has also contributed
to the strain on the system. Absolutely, we've said it many times,
there have been disproportionate reactions. That's part of the issue as well.
But from Israel’s perspective, Iran clearly represents a threat,
a systemic one. Because Iran openly states that it wants to destroy Israel.
So clearly, when someone says they want to destroy you, and is developing
a nuclear weapon, you perceive that as a very serious threat. Right? - Guys, there's a problem
- It was a technical issue. It's the Iranians... Isn’t our foreign policy too dependent on the United States and therefore Trump? Do you mean this government’s
policy, or in general? Italy's foreign policy in general I think it's undeniable that not only Italian, but European foreign policy has been
heavily influenced, over the past 80 years, by the US. But then we should ask ourselves why.
What always surprises me is that those who complain about excessive
American influence, are often the same people who complain when we try to strengthen
our own defense. Now, I think it’s time to understand something simple: if you ask
someone to defend you, to be responsible - for your safety, they don't do it for free.
 - Of course - They don't do it for free.
 Especially the US Nobody does it for free.
This gives them influence. Which is why I, as someone who considers herself
a patriot, and while pursuing a strongly pro-Western foreign policy,
for reasons we can talk about I've been the only leader in this country who,
even while in opposition, had the courage to say we must invest
in our own ability to defend ourselves. Because the resources we invest
in defense are the price of our autonomy. They are the price of our freedom.
We either understand this, or we accept the reality we know.
Now, I asked if you were talking about Italy’s foreign policy in general
or this government's foreign policy. I work toward an Italy
that is fully independent, fully capable of standing on its own.
Today, this is an issue that concerns Europe. We've always talked
about a European pillar within NATO Meaning the ability to operate
within the Atlantic Alliance on equal footing. But that depends on the strength of each country.
That said, I firmly believe it's in the interest of both Italy
and Europe to strengthen cooperation within the Western and Euro-Atlantic framework,
rather than encouraging the centrifugal forces we’re currently seeing.
Not because it benefits the Americans, but because it benefits us.
Especially if you consider the alternatives. The main alternative
is a growing Chinese influence in Europe. This is my point of view. You're free to disagree. You just said "independent" In what areas are we independent?
We have problems with immigration, huge problems--as we’re seeing right now--\ with oil and defense.
So, at best, ,we have someone helping us with defense. And we're closely tied
to the US when it comes to external threats and therefore to NATO.
So what does Italy control? And Europe Italy controls a lot of things.
Let’s not exaggerate. What is true is that Europe does have
a problem with strategic autonomy. And we have this problem because, frankly,
we’ve neglected key areas for decades. Defense, raw materials, energy...
We were comfortable in our bubble depending on the United States for security,
on Russia for energy, and on China for raw materials.Then
the shocks hit: the pandemic, the war in Ukraine, now the tensions with Iran,
and the issues we face in Africa... Even going back to Gheddafi. Yeah ok, we can go back as much as you want, but-- Libya was highly relevant, in terms of energy
and immigration, right? It was, It was relevant but
the war in Ukraine had a much greater impact. Because we depended on Russian gas
for over 40%. And overnight, that supply was gone.
So yes, we could give more examples, but take the pandemic:
from one day to the next, we realized, while we were heavily
investing in electrification-- which clearly ties us immensely
to another giant: China, for microchips, semiconductors...
And when the pandemic hit, China prioritized its own market.
They turned off the tap, and the entire supply chains stopped.
The same goes for defense. As we said, the debate in Europe around
the so-called strategic autonomy is exactly about this.
 And the things I talk about, for example the raw materials issue,
or our cooperation with Africa, are also linked to supply security. Because if you want to control
your supply chains, you have to try, --if you don't have those materials--
to rely on friend-shoring or near-shoring. That means
working with countries hat are close to you, or that you trust more. Today are we starting to move
in that direction But isn't it a bit too late? Nuclear energy was another mistake It was. And we are now reopening
that discussion. As you know, this government
has brought back the nuclear topic If we want an energy policy
that protects us from these shocks, what do we need to do?
We need to diversify as much as possible. Diversify our sources,
the types of energy-- The investments And our suppliers. We've done a lot.
Italy has done a lot in recent years. It didn’t start with this government,
but with the previous one Especially after the war in Ukraine.
Today, we're safe from major supply shocks. But we're not safe from price increases. We'’re seeing it right now. If you want an effective energy policy,
you need to diversify, invest in research, and develop new technologies.This is
the principle of technological neutrality that we are trying to promote in Europe,
where there is still an ideological approach to these issues. When Europe decided
to pursue the green transition, the problem wasn’t the goal itself,
but the fact that it dictated which technologies we had to use.
And the main focus was electrification. But that ties us completely
to another geopolitical giant-- Which raises a number of questions... Exactly, it does. Especially since we know it's one of the most
polluting countries in the world. So it doesn’t make much sense
to reduce emissions in Europe by 5% if the technology you rely on
is produced using coal plants. They’re called global emissions for a reason. If they go down here and rise elsewhere,
there are still global emissions. And as you were saying,
no one acts out of philanthropy. Exactly. So, a number of strategies
were flawed and they're being corrected. Thank God. When someone raised these issues
before all these shocks happened And I was one of them--
they were labeled as “sovereigntists” or accused of wanting to go backwards. But in life you have to be pragmatic,
because mistakes have consequences and we're now paying for them. Bringing it back to today,
oil prices are going to go up We started at around $60 a barrel, and they could reach $160.
Is there a strategy to deal with this now? Right now, after two weeks, we're mainly focusing on monitoring.
We have strengthened our price monitoring system,
especially when it comes to fuel prices.
It means involving the Financial Police more
and the relevant authorities. Because at a certain point,
if prices stabilize --I'll explain how--
you have to intervene. Yeah, I saw that in Germany, fuel prices
have increased much more than in Italy Yeah, that's why.
And not only in Germany, in most European countries prices have risen more
than here. That’s because we are monitoring the situation closely. It means that
the Financial Police are out there checking. Because my concern is this:
once prices stabilize, I need to step in by allocating public funds.
And we should always remember, it's the money of the people who pay taxes.
So before spending it I wanna make sure I'm not handing over billions
or millions of euros to people speculating on the crisis.
So first we must curb speculation then we can intervene,
once the prices stabilize. How? With this tool called
“floating excise duties.” We've had it since 2008
and we reformed it in 2023 with the fuel decree. In simple terms, when fuel prices rise
above a certain level, the government collects more VAT
from higher prices. So we offset that increase
by lowering excise taxes, bringing prices back down.
But this only works if the increase is structural.
If prices spike for just a few days, the extra VAT revenue is minimal,
so the impact would be barely noticeable. That’s the first tool we can use.
If we need more resources, we’ll assess that
within the broader public finance framework. I want to ask a question about a topic
we’ve discussed in past episodes Article 31 of the security decree.
 Let me read it: Article 31 includes provisions that make
intelligence agents not punishable for certain acts that would otherwise
be considered criminal. Article 31 specifically allows
the leadership and organization of terrorist groups, including international
ones or those aimed at undermining the democratic order, as well as the production
and possession of explosives. When we read this,
it honestly made us a bit uneasy, because historically in this country, allowing
intelligence services to handle explosives, has not always ended well.
Should we be worried about these superpowers we're giving them? No, I don’t think so. I think it’s important to keep
n mind that when an intelligence officer infiltrates a terrorist organization,
they’re not creating a threat they’re trying to prevent one.
And let's not forget these people are risking their lives
every single minute. So please, let’s not distort reality.
We’re talking about thousands of people whose names and faces we may never know.
Who may never receive recognition, and who risk their lives daily to protect ours. That said, regarding the decree,
there are a few key points to keep in mind.
First, intelligence agencies as we call them, cannot act on their own They need authorization
from the competent authority. That’s the first safeguard.
Second, this is not about granting “superpowers.”
These are operational tools and they’re not new. They already existed they're just being updated,
because terrorism itself is evolving We used to deal with structured groups,
like the Red Brigades, with a clear, structured, almost monolithic
hierarchy. That was one thing Today, the kind of terrorism we face
is very different. For example, take Islamist extremism,
it’s mostly lone actors or small cells It’s a completely different model
So simply saying 'you can infiltrate' is no longer enough.
That’s why we're updating the tools If we want intelligence to be effective,
we have to equip it properly. Not because they want to attack us
but because they want to prevent attacks. That's a very different thing. I mean, I've already said it with Tajani, I don't think it makes sense
to talk about this topic, because how do you ensure transparency
with intelligence services? It comes down to trust You either trust institutions or you don't That said, we’ve learned that in any field,
there can be people who are 'bad' or who misuse their power. But that doesn’t mean everything else
is corrupted. I see it every day. Things you will never know about,
attacks that were prevented, lives that were protected,
things that can’t even be disclosed, carried out by people who will never hear
a simple “well done.” I agree with you,
but we shouldn’t underestimate the risk. Of course. And we nee to be very strict
with those who misuse their power. - Cause we have a history
-It's been hard to hold them accountable That can happen in any field.
But we’re talking about one case out of millions. So we need to keep things in perspective - Let’s move on to the referendum.
- Which one? - The referendum on justice.
- Good The first question is,
 Why do you think this referendum is turning into a political clash, instead of focusing
on the core of the reform? Is this becoming a referendum
against the government? Well, the “No” camp wants it to be against
the government. They struggle to engage with the substance of the proposal, because,
first of all, it's common sense. Second, many of those opposing it today
have supported similar positions in the past. So, since they can’t really
argue against the reform, the only strategy they have
is to rally voters by saying “vote against Meloni.”
I think this is a trap even for those who strongly oppose me. Because this is not a vote on Meloni,
it’s a vote on the justice system If you dislike me but agree with the reform,
you should vote 'yes' now and vote against me next year
in the next general election which is when you actually vote
on governments and parties. In the meantime,you could secure a reform
that improves the justice system in Italy As for me, even if the “No” side wins,
I've already said it I will complete my mandate,
finish the work, and face voters to be judged on the results. My concern is this: if you vote “no” today just to get rid of me,
you may end up with both: Me still in office and a system that doesn't work
Doesn't sound good, huh? So my advice is: secure a better justice system
now, regardless of who is in power, and then run your campaign
to vote me out at the election. You learned from Renzi. Right, she's being smarter than Renzi No, I just don't agree Because this is not about the government
I know that even among left-wing voters, including
the radical left--who won't vote-- many actually agree with this reform.
We've discussed it for years and it has always been cross-party
You can see it today, plenty of people from the left--
Just yesterday I shared a video of Stefano Ceccanti, a leading figure
in the Democratic Party who has always supported it. He’s voting “yes.”
 The Vice-President of the European Parliament, Pina Picierno,
also from the Democratic Party. Paola Concia, and many magistrates and legal experts
So it would make no sense to turn this into something else.
But I understand why others try Because when you struggle
to find flaws, you need a different narrative to mobilize voters. Right? We’ve had guests on this podcast like Colombo, Gratteri,
and Di Pietro, and we’ve discussed this referendum at length. Why do supporters of
the “Yes” side think that separating the careers of judges and prosecutors
improves judicial impartiality? Well, the point is this:
if the person who prosecutes you and the one who judges you
have overlapping career paths, it’s reasonable to assume
that the judge may give more weight to what the prosecutor says. And this isn’t
just theory. Let me give you some numbers. Do you know how often judges approve
prosecutors requests? Do you? For example.. Requests to validate
--I don't know--arrests 95%. Requests to extend wiretaps, 99%. Overall, across different types of requests,
approval rates range between 93% and 99%. So either prosecutors in Italy are phenomenal or there’s a natural tendency
to trust someone you know. Someone you’ve worked with.
And that’s human. Relationships influence us.
So by separating career paths, you reduce that risk.
So as the Constitution itself requires since everybody talks about
"defending" the Constitution we have to strengthen the judge’s role
as an independent and impartial arbiter. And since you can't really argue with this,
people started talking about an “illiberal drift,”
an attack on the Constitution. But then, you look around Europe
and see that in at least 21 out of 27 EU countries, these careers are already separate.
So help me understand. I've always been told I should align with Europe
cause I wasn’t pro-European enough and now that I am,
I’m being accused of an “illiberal drift.” So is everyone else in Europe illiberal,
or are we the ones who are behind? I believe the second, and it's time to move forward Since we don't have much time, I’d like to focus on the critics of this reform. I’d like to say something. I'm truly saddened cause I find the level
of communication on both sides quite disturbing. I used to work in advertising and I know
communication is manipulation but in this case on both sides
there has been a serious level of manipulation. I've been trying to focus
on the content of the reform because what we’re voting
on March 22nd and 23rd is not about politics. It doesn’t affect me,
nor the government, or any political party. It affects citizens and the state
of the justice system in this country. We have to keep this in mind.
For a country to function, there are three fundamental powers and the judiciary
is one of them. And it impacts people’s lives everyday: immigration, security, health,
personal freedom, work. If that system doesn't work I'm telling you--as part of another branch of power--
the whole mechanism breaks down I'm worried that
this will be very different in reality... Why? Because your party--and the entire majority
Are saying: “If you vote yes, this is what will happen…”
But in reality, there will be adjustments,
a rebalancing of power. And that’s fine-- Wait, no. No, let me-- But some of the examples used
in the campaign on both sides won’t actually change. And I find this let's say misleading.
Also unfair to the public. Let me be clear:
this is not about power structures. It’s about merit. It’s about efficiency. The main issue we’re addressing
is that in Italy we have a system where,
even when something goes wrong, nothing really happens
And citizens end up paying the price. If you select members of the High Council of
the Judiciary, based on ideological, factional, or political criteria, you'll end up
with people deciding who gets promoted, who gets sanctioned,
and who gets transferred not based on merit, but on affiliation. And that creates a serious efficiency problem. Let me give you two examples. In one case,
a judge delayed the release of a detainee by one year and seven months.
One year and seven months. The case went to the CSM, the High Council
and what was the assessment? “Of limited relevance.” One year and 7 months
of a person's life. Limited relevance?! And the judge still received
a positive career evaluation. Another case: a judge with repeated delays in filing rulings. You know that a ruling only becomes effective once it is formally filed,
not when it is read in court? Ok. There were around 60 instances of delay some of them close to four years.
And this was a family court judge. Four years. We’re talking about decisions
that affect children’s lives So the ruling is announced when a child is three, but it becomes effective
when that child is seven. 60 cases. The outcome? Everything was swept under the rug
and a positive evaluation for promotion. The issue is this, as Di Pietro says, that the evaluated
and the evaluators operate on the same level. The evaluated is the one selecting
the evaluator. Guys, the evaluated appoints the evaluator.
So of course, if you were chosen by those people you are influenced by them.
And if you’ve been backed by a faction, you’re even more influenced.
Because in many cases that faction will tell you what it expects from you.
But if you are randomly selected, those pressures disappear.
And in a system where judges are evaluated, promoted, and transferred based on merit,
everything becomes more efficient And when the system improves,
it’s not me who benefits, it's the citizens Look, you’re speaking to someone who has
personally experienced these issues. I’ve been through the courts,
I’ve spent a lot of money lawyers are expensive,we all know that.
I’m not speaking as an outsider. My point was mainly
about the communication. Because ok, these are two examples
but there are also many cases where prosecutors and judges
have shown real competence, even today. - What I'm saying is, why do we have--
- Of course! Wait, can I just add one thing? - That's true. But have you asked--
You said it, the goal is meritocracy Have you asked yourself why
so many highly respected magistrates are fighting for this reform? And why many more
will vote 'yes' than those who openly say so? Because this reform is not against magistrates
It’s actually for them Not just those who were part
of a certain system, but also those who have been sidelined,
who’ve seen others move ahead - for reasons unrelated to merit.
- What I'm saying is that since parts of this reform are still missing.
We've seen the proposal that’s been approved, but it's not complete, I often see arguments
--from the “No” side as well--that are hypothetical. Your narrative, understandably, is: "by voting Yes
we’ll move toward meritocracy,” But from a citizen’s perspective,
people have also been pushed - to decide emotionally, on impulse.
- You're talking about the campaign? - Both campaigns
 - I’m not sure I agree, You mentioned the case of 'the robber'...
But what does it have to do with the reform? Let's address it. People like Gratteri and
Colombo, who have been our guests, say that the random selection of so-called
lay members could actually be influenced - by politics. Is that really the case?
- Yes. - Please...
- No, I meant of course you wouldn't say yes Let me explain.
Do you know how lay members are currently selected by Parliament?
Because Gratteri knows. And Colombo knows too. Let me walk you through it.
Parliament has to appoint ten lay members. Ideally all at once, but that doesn’t
always happen. And this is how it works: political parties, or rather, party leaders
sit down and divide them up. Each party nominates its own representatives,
based on their political weight. So I call Elly Schlein, she calls Giuseppe Conte
and we reach an agreement. “You get two names, I get two,
someone else gets one…” Does that sound detached from politics to you?
Of course not. It’s a system where parties appoint their own people to the CSM.
And the Vice President of the CSM, while the President of the Republic
formally presides over it, is the one who runs day-to-day operations,
and is chosen from among those lay members. Let’s recall who has held
that role over the past 25 years. Giovanni Legnini, a former
undersecretary to the Prime Minister under the Renzi government, and a PD member.
It'd be like me appointing Alfredo Mantovano. Michele Vietti, a former MP for the CCD. Davide Ermini,
a formerMP for the PD and head of justice policy for the Democratic Party. Nicola Mancino, a former
Interior Minister under the Amato government. It'd be like me appointing Piantedosi
Do you think politics is not involved? I find it amusing when people act as if
politics has had nothing to do with the CSM. What we’re building now
is a completely different system. A system where political parties, both in the
majority and in the opposition, draw up a long list of qualified candidates,
of course they have to be qualified and then names are selected at random
from that list. So political influence - is significantly reduced.
- There are ten lay members, right? Yes, and I’ll add something else
In the implementing legislation we should include a rule
preventing politicians at least for a certain period,
from serving on the CSM. That would further limit political influence,
which is precisely the goal of this reform. Another issue that gets
little attention is the High Court. Could you explain how it would work? The High Court is a body that would take over
disciplinary authority from the current CSM. That power would be transferred
to a new institution, composed mainly of judges, with a smaller share of lay members
selected by Parliament through a random draw. But their role would be reduced because today,
 lay members account for one third In the High Court, they would be one-fifth.
Three out of fifteen. These members would also be selected by
a random draw both from the judicial side and the lay side. And this body would operate
with full independence, without having to answer to anyone
when handling disciplinary cases such as negligence, misconduct,and so on.
For the first time in Italy’s history judges who make mistakes would be evaluated
by an independent body, which is normal. And this is something people rarely talk about,
but in 1987, a referendum with over 80% support, approved civil liability
for judges. And yet, that has been forgotten. Because in Italy it's been almost impossible
to reform the justice system.
Not because nobody's tried. But nothing stays the same forever and we need to evolve, right?
In these 80 years we've reformed almost everything: the government
the regions, the state budget... We've reformed every area imaginable.
But the justice system has never really been touched.
Not in any meaningful way. - But there have been reforms on justice
- Yeah, very very small ones Every time a more serious reform was attempted,
there was this backlash you're seeing now. And people say this reform
threatens the separation of powers But Parliament’s role is to make laws.
If you claim it can't, that's a problem Back in the Berlusconi years, it was easier
to frame this as a political clash The situation was different, but with Renzi
it was the same thing Left or right. Anyone who's tried
to address this issue. - For historical reasons, maybe...
 - No, because there’s no real willingness to engage in dialogue on this topic.
It's always the same reaction: a knee-jerk reaction. The problem is, when you want
